Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key clinical findings and impression:
  - Abrupt 4-day history of severe pruritus with sore, red, dry, partly cracked skin on chest, hands and antecubital fossae. Symptoms severe enough to disrupt sleep and concentration at work.
  - Past history of eczema; physician viewed rash and described it as familiar.
  - No systemic features reported (no fever, cough, breathing difficulty). No pus, bleeding, or discharge documented.
- Working diagnosis (supported by transcript and DDx): Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare — High likelihood. Justification: prior eczema history, typical distribution (antecubital fossae/arms and trunk), dry/cracked skin, intense pruritus; treating clinician also suspected eczema and recommended topical steroid and emollients (DDx ranked this as highest likelihood).
- Management plan documented in transcript:
  - Prescription/plan for a stronger topical steroid (specific agent/dose not documented).
  - Emollient recommended for use in bath/shower for 7–10 days (product/dose not documented).
  - Consideration of antihistamines for itch control; doctor offered prescription-strength option (fexofenadine) — dose/route/frequency not documented. Patient reports prior antihistamines did not help (type unspecified).
  - Advise keeping a diary of potential triggers (soap, shower gels, clothing) and avoid potential irritants.
  - Return review: come back in 1 week if no improvement.
- Relevant differentials from DDx consistent with transcript:
  - Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis — Medium likelihood. Acute, itchy, widespread rash possible if exposed to a new product; patient unsure about triggers.
  - Scabies infestation — Medium likelihood. Severe nocturnal itch and involvement of hands/trunk with household contacts possible; classic burrows/typical distribution not documented.
  - Xerosis with eczematization — Medium likelihood as a contributing/exacerbating factor.
  - Secondary bacterial infection — Low likelihood (no purulence, systemic signs).
- Considerations: monitor response to prescribed topical steroid and emollient over 7–10 days; if poor response or atypical features, consider skin examination in person, scabies assessment, and swab if infection suspected.

Health Promotion & Planning

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification: Advised use of emollients regularly, avoid identified triggers, and use topical steroid as prescribed; antihistamines may be tried for symptomatic relief. (Documented in transcript.)
- Patient health goals and priorities: Patient seeks rapid symptom relief to restore sleep and ability to work and resume activities such as hiking.
- Eligibility for GP Management Plan (GPMP) or Team Care Arrangements (TCA): Not recorded.
- Referrals (allied health, Quitline, AOD services, Aboriginal health worker, or social supports): Not recorded.
- Follow-up and recall appointments scheduled: Advised to return in 1 week if symptoms do not improve.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare — High likelihood. Prior eczema, typical distribution (antecubital fossae/arms and chest), dry/cracked skin, severe pruritus; treating clinician reached same impression and recommended topical steroid + emollients.
- Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis — Medium likelihood. Acute, intensely itchy rash can follow exposure to new soaps, detergents, clothing or topical agents; patient uncertain about recent exposures.
- Scabies infestation — Medium likelihood. Severe nocturnal pruritus and involvement of hands and trunk with household contacts are compatible; absence of documented burrows or classic distribution reduces specificity.

Quality checks
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs (BP, pulse), focused skin examination details (morphology of lesions, presence/absence of burrows, distribution maps), lesion photographs or dermatology description, height/weight/BMI, immunisation review, medication names/doses/routes/frequencies, any laboratory or swab testing, and formal documentation of trigger exposures or contact history.
- Internal conflicts or contradictions between transcript and DDx: None noted.
- Transcript quality notes: Audio quality was poor at times (clinician commented on sound quality); portions of the dialogue were unclear or interrupted. Some medication names/doses were not specified.
